ITEM 4. INFORMATION ON THE COMPANY
A. History and Development of the Company
We are an Israeli corporation based in Israel
and were incorporated on June 30, 2013, under the name ParaZero Ltd. On September 6, 2018, our name was changed to ParaZero
Israel Ltd., and on November 4, 2018, our name was changed to our current name, ParaZero Technologies Ltd. Our principal executive
offices are located at 1 Hatachana Street, Kfar Saba, 4453001, Israel. Our telephone number in Israel is +972-50-275-3666. Our website
address is www.parazero.com. The information contained on our website and available through our website is not incorporated
by reference into and should not be considered a part of this Annual Report, and the reference to our website in this Annual Report is
an inactive textual reference only.
We have incurred net losses since our inception,
including net losses of $5,412,163 and $11,054,230 for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024, respectively. As a result,
we had accumulated losses of $34,889,450 as of December 31, 2025. We anticipate that we will continue to incur significant losses
for the foreseeable future as our operating expenses and capital expenditures increase substantially due to our continued investment in
research and development as well as in sales and marketing activities and as we hire additional employees over the coming years.
B. Business Overview
Overview
ParaZero Technologies Ltd.
is an Israel-based aerospace and defense technology company focused on safety, protection, and mitigation solutions for unmanned aerial
systems, or UAS. We were founded in 2014 with the objective of enabling the safe and scalable integration of drones into regulated airspace
and sensitive operational environments.
Our technological foundation
is rooted in aerospace-grade engineering, autonomous safety mechanisms, and real-time flight monitoring systems. Since our inception,
we have focused on addressing one of the key barriers to drone adoption: the risk posed to people, property, and critical infrastructure
in the event of system failure or loss of control.
Over time, we have developed
a portfolio of proprietary technologies designed to autonomously respond to emergency scenarios. This legacy of safety-centric design,
operational data, and field deployment experience has positioned us to expand beyond commercial applications into defense and security-oriented
markets, applying the same patent technology to create counter-UAS, or C-UAS solutions, also known as anti-drone solutions.
The rapid adoption of UAS
technologies in recent years has also introduced significant security challenges. UAS technology is now easily accessible not only to
militaries around the world but also to non-state entities, criminal organizations, and individuals with malicious intent.
After years of saving
numerous unmanned and manned aerial systems, we applied our innovative, patent-protected technology in order to lead the battle against
hostile drones. We believe that our technology solutions leverage a distinct technology portfolio protected by global patents that were
developed over the course of more than a decade. We believe that this technology portfolio enables us to effectively counteract various
threats posed by drones by rapidly developing bespoke C-UAS solutions for key clientele. Recent international conflicts have highlighted
the extensive use of drones in various attacks and the critical necessity to counteract these strikes promptly with minimal damage as
well as deliver critical supplies in high-risk operational zones. We have commenced development of dedicated solutions based on our technology.
Industry Overview and Market Potential
UAS and C-UAS Markets
UASs have evolved from niche
platforms into mainstream tools used by government, defense, and commercial operators to collect data, deliver services, and improve operational
efficiency. The UAS value chain typically includes (i) airframes and propulsion systems, (ii) payloads such as electro-optical/infrared,
or EO/IR, cameras and other sensors, (iii) communications links, (iv) ground control software and mission planning, and (v) data processing,
analytics and integration into customer workflows. Demand continues to be shaped by improvements in autonomy, edge computing, sensor miniaturization,
endurance, and secure communications, as well as expanding use cases across public safety, critical infrastructure, border and coastal
monitoring, industrial inspection, mapping, and logistics. According to Fortune Business Insights, the global UAS market was valued at
$41.27 billion in 2025 and is project to grow to $160.44 billion by 2034, exhibiting a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of 16.40%
during the forecast period. The growth in the UAS market is growing primarily due to increased military and defense spending, expanding
commercial applications across industries, advancements in autonomous drone technologies, and the demonstrated efficiency of drones in
critical logistics and operational support functions.
37
In parallel, the proliferation
of low-cost, widely available UAS has created a growing need for C-UAS solutions to detect, identify, track, and mitigate unauthorized
drones. C-UAS systems are deployed to protect sensitive locations and operations, including airports, military bases, government facilities,
prisons, energy assets, public events, and critical infrastructure. C-UAS solutions typically combine multiple sensor types—such
as radar, radio-frequency, or RF, detection, EO/IR, and acoustic sensors—with command-and-control software that fuses sensor data,
supports identification (including distinguishing drones from birds or other objects), and enables response options. Mitigation capabilities
may include non-kinetic measures (e.g., RF disruption, protocol manipulation, navigation spoofing, and other electronic effects where
lawful) and kinetic or physical capture methods, often subject to strict legal and operational constraints. According to recent report
by Grand View Research, the global anti-drone market size was estimated at $3,180.9 million in 2025 and is projected to reach $19,844.5
million by 2033, growing at a CAGR of 25.2% from 2026 to 2033. The market is primarily driven by the rising demand for UAS technology
and the escalating concerns regarding security threats posed by unauthorized drone activities.
We believe the market opportunity
for UAS and C-UAS solutions is significant and expanding, driven by increasing adoption of drones for commercial, governmental, and defense
applications, as well as heightened security concerns related to unauthorized or malicious drone activity. UAS adoption is supported by
the ability to reduce costs, improve safety, and enhance data collection across a range of use cases, while the growing number and sophistication
of drone-related incidents is increasing demand for airspace awareness, site protection, and layered defense capabilities.
The C-UAS market, in particular,
is driven by the need to protect critical infrastructure, public venues, borders, and sensitive facilities through integrated detection,
identification, tracking, and mitigation solutions. Customers increasingly seek scalable, interoperable systems that combine multiple
sensor modalities with centralized command-and-control software and can integrate into existing security architectures. Although procurement
cycles and regulatory considerations may affect deployment timelines, we believe long-term growth will be supported by continued drone
proliferation, technological advancements such as AI-enabled detection and sensor fusion, and sustained government and enterprise investment
in airspace security.
Commercial Drone Market
The global use of commercial
drones has expanded rapidly across a wide range of industries, including infrastructure inspection, public safety, logistics, agriculture,
and media production. As drone operations increasingly occur over populated areas, urban environments, and critical infrastructure, regulators
worldwide have introduced more stringent operational and safety requirements. Growth is driven by advances in autonomy, sensor technology,
battery performance, and data analytics, which enhance operational efficiency, reduce costs, and improve safety compared to traditional
manned alternatives. As regulatory frameworks mature and integration with enterprise software ecosystems improves, commercial drones are
becoming a core tool for data acquisition and real-time decision-making across multiple industries.
According to Future Market
Insights, the global commercial drone market size was valued at $45,288.1 million in 2025 and is expected to reach $1,176.9 million
by 2035. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of 28.2% from 2025 to 2035, driven by the increasing use of drones to improve
efficiency, reduce costs and gather aerial data for tasks like mapping, surveying, logistics, inspection and monitoring, while
advances in drone technology, software and services make drones more useful and accessible to businesses.
Aviation
authorities in major markets, including the United States and Europe, require drone operators to demonstrate effective mitigation of
ground risk as a condition for advanced operational approvals, such as flights over people, beyond visual line of sight, BVLOS,
operations, and operations in controlled or congested airspace.
38
As a result, regulatory compliance
has become a key enabler for commercial drone deployment at scale. Technologies that actively reduce risk to people and property are increasingly
viewed as necessary components of compliant drone operations rather than optional enhancements.
Drone Delivery Market
The drone delivery market represents a rapidly
emerging segment of the broader commercial drone industry, focused on transporting lightweight goods such as food, medical supplies, e-commerce
parcels, and critical spare parts. According to Statista by 2030, the global drone delivery market is projected to generate over $4.9
billion in revenue.
Adoption is driven by the potential to reduce
delivery times, lower last-mile logistics costs, expand access in remote or congested areas, and enhance service reliability. Pilot programs
and limited commercial operations are underway in multiple jurisdictions, supported by advances in navigation, detect-and-avoid systems,
fleet management software, and automated ground infrastructure.
Market expansion remains
closely tied to regulatory approvals, airspace integration frameworks, public acceptance, and the development of scalable operational
models. As aviation authorities continue to establish rules for BVLOS operations and urban air mobility corridors, industry participants
are investing in redundant safety systems, traffic management integration, and partnerships with retailers, healthcare providers, and
logistics operators. Over time, broader regulatory clarity and continued technological maturation are expected to support increased commercialization
and network-scale deployments.
Drone Safety Incidents and Threats
Commercial drones offer significant
value to private industry and the public sector and are flying in ever-increasing numbers in the skies. As the global utilization of drones
grows at an increasing rate, we expect the number of safety incidents to increase as well. Drones routinely experience mid-flight emergencies,
including electrical system failures, bird strikes, excessive angular breach or altitude loss, etc., and can fall out of the sky and can
be part of safety incidents such as collisions with other flying objects or structures. For example, the European Aviation Safety Agency,
or EASA, reported that in 2023 a total of 12 UAS accidents and serious incidents happened.
Advancement in drone technology
has created threats on defense forces, national security and critical infrastructure through the use of advanced drones. Such drones,
while being armed, are capable of attacks. Such incidents have reportedly increased in recent years, and hence security threats have led
governments to think of anti-drone technologies. The increasing use of military and non-military drones for attacks on defense and civilian
infrastructure and establishments as well as the use of drones for criminal activity, like smuggling, has necessitated the need for counter
drone technology.
The utilization of UAS has
become a global security concern, transcending geographic and conflict boundaries. According to recent research by Chávez and Swed,
over 65 criminal, insurgent or terrorist organizations now possess the capability to deploy drones. This broad adoption underscores the
pivotal role drones play in modern warfare and security breaches.
The Drone Threat on Defense Forces, Homeland
Security and Commercial Assests
Small drones have emerged
as a serious and rapidly evolving threat to both critical infrastructure and military forces worldwide. Their low cost, widespread availability,
and ease of modification allow state and non-state actors to conduct surveillance, disruption, and precision attacks with minimal resources
and limited warning. Critical infrastructure sites such as power stations, substations, refineries, water treatment facilities, and transportation
hubs are particularly vulnerable, as even small payloads or kinetic impact can disable exposed components and trigger cascading system
failures. For armies, small drones have transformed the battlefield by eroding traditional advantages in armor, concealment, and fixed
defenses; they enable persistent aerial surveillance, accurate targeting, and low-cost strike capabilities that place troops and bases
under constant overhead threat. The combination of operational effectiveness, psychological impact, and difficulty of detection makes
small drones a structural security challenge, requiring new doctrines, technologies, and protective measures to defend both civilian infrastructure
and military assets.
39
In 2025 there were various
threats made by drones such as: Critical infrastructure (energy grids, airports, fuel depots) that were disabled or disrupted by relatively
inexpensive drone systems. Airspace safety around major civilian hubs has been compromised, leading to airport closures and travel disruption.
Military operations and bases are under persistent threat from cheap, proliferated UAVs in active warzones and civilians outside conflict
zones were harmed by drone activity in urban areas.
Our Strategy
Autonomous Drone Safety System as the Answer to Regulators Worldwide
Our SafeAir system was developed
in direct response to regulatory requirements governing commercial drone operations in populated and sensitive environments. Aviation
authorities worldwide require operators to demonstrate effective mitigation of ground risk as a condition for advanced operational approvals,
including flights over people, BVLOS operations, and operations in congested or controlled airspace.
SafeAir is designed to function
as an autonomous safety layer that reduces the risk posed by a drone in the event of a critical failure. The system continuously monitors
flight parameters and system behavior and, upon detecting predefined emergency conditions, autonomously initiates a controlled descent
sequence. By reducing impact energy and limiting uncontrolled descent, SafeAir is intended to mitigate potential harm to people and property
on the ground.
A key regulatory consideration
addressed by SafeAir is independence from the drone’s primary flight control systems. SafeAir operates as a self-contained system
designed to activate even in scenarios involving severe system malfunction, loss of control, or power failure. This architectural separation
aligns with regulatory expectations for fail-safe or fail-operational safety mechanisms in aviation systems.
Regulatory frameworks in major
markets emphasize outcome-based safety objectives rather than prescriptive design requirements. SafeAir is intended to support these objectives
by providing a measurable and repeatable method of ground risk reduction. In regulatory assessments, such mitigation measures may be used
by operators as part of their safety cases, risk analyses, and operational approval submissions.
As commercial drone operations
expand into higher-risk environments, the presence of an autonomous safety system such as SafeAir may enable operators to pursue broader
operational authorizations while maintaining compliance with applicable safety regulations. SafeAir has therefore become a core component
of our commercial offering and a foundational element of the our technology portfolio.
40
Strategic Transition to the Defense Sector and Evolving Drone
Threat Landscape
Building on our safety-focused technological heritage,
we have expanded our activities into the defense and homeland security sectors in response to the rapidly evolving use of drones as tools
of conflict, disruption, and asymmetric warfare.
Over the past decade, drones—particularly
small, commercially derived platforms—have become widely accessible, inexpensive, and increasingly capable. These systems are now
routinely used by state and non-state actors for intelligence collection, targeting, harassment, disruption of critical infrastructure,
and direct kinetic attacks. The proliferation of first-person-view, or FPV, attack drones has further intensified this threat by enabling
high-speed, low-altitude attacks with minimal warning and short engagement timelines.
Traditional air defense systems were not designed
to counter these threats effectively. Missile-based interceptors and conventional air defense assets are often impractical or economically
unsustainable against small drones, particularly in close-range scenarios or populated environments. Electronic warfare solutions may
be ineffective against autonomous drones, pre-programmed flight paths, or systems employing alternative communication methods.
As a result, defense and security organizations
increasingly require C-UAS solutions that are cost-effective, rapidly deployable, and suitable for use in urban, civilian, and sensitive
environments. There is growing demand for systems that can provide a controlled, close-range kinetic response while minimizing collateral
damage and operational risk.
Our strategic transition into the defense sector
is driven by this evolving threat landscape and our ability to apply its core competencies—autonomous activation, rapid-response
safety mechanisms, and controlled kinetic intervention—to defense applications. We have leveraged our experience in safety-critical
aerospace systems to develop C-UAS solutions specifically designed to address modern drone threats at close range.
This transition expands our
addressable market beyond commercial drone safety into defense, homeland security, and critical infrastructure protection. These markets
are characterized by increasing procurement activity, evolving operational requirements, and sustained demand driven by the persistent
and adaptive nature of drone-based threats.
Business Strategy
We are implementing a multi-tiered
business model to increase flexibility in the market and to encourage broad adoption of our products in the defense / homeland security
and commercial drone markets. A portion of our defense and commercial solutions are sold directly to original equipment manufacturers,
or OEMs, which usually are characterized by long sales cycles and in the commercial drone market are also original design manufacturers,
or ODMs. Defense OEMs are usually the solution provider for the end users. Our direct interaction with OEMs enables us to work with them
from the design stage, providing for seamless integration of our solutions into their products. We also market our solutions directly
to clients via direct sales, resellers and an online store.
41
Our Solutions
C-UAS Solutions and the DefendAir Product
Portfolio
Overview of C-UAS Solutions
C-UAS solutions are generally
categorized into two primary approaches: soft-kill and hard-kill.
Soft-kill solutions typically
rely on electronic warfare techniques such as radio-frequency jamming, GNSS interference, or cyber-based takeover of the target drone.
These methods are designed to disrupt communication or navigation links and may be effective against certain classes of drones. However,
their effectiveness can be limited against autonomous drones, pre-programmed flight paths, or systems employing alternative communication
methods.
Hard-kill solutions involve
the physical neutralization of a hostile drone through kinetic or explosive means. These approaches may include projectiles, missiles,
or other intercept mechanisms. While effective in some scenarios, traditional hard-kill systems may introduce risks related to collateral
damage, debris, cost asymmetry, and suitability for use in populated or sensitive environments.
Modern C-UAS architectures
increasingly employ a layered approach that combines detection, tracking, soft-kill measures, and a final kinetic interception layer to
address residual threats.
DefendAir – Net-Based C-UAS Technology
Our DefendAir is a non-explosive,
net-based C-UAS solution designed to physically intercept and neutralize hostile drones at close range. The system engages incoming aerial
threats by deploying a specialized net that entangles the target drone, disrupting its propulsion system, flight control, and aerodynamic
stability, thereby preventing continued controlled operation.
42
Unlike explosive or projectile-based
interception methods, DefendAir is designed to deliver a controlled kinetic response that does not rely on blast effects or high-energy
munitions. This design approach is intended to reduce the risk of collateral damage, limit secondary hazards from debris, and avoid unintended
effects on surrounding personnel, infrastructure, or civilian environments. As a result, DefendAir may be suitable for deployment in locations
where the use of conventional hard-kill systems is restricted or operationally undesirable.
The net-based interception
mechanism reflects our experience in autonomous activation, precision deployment, and safety-critical aerospace system design. The system
is engineered to deliver a predictable and contained interception outcome, aligning with operational requirements for close-range defense
and controlled engagement in complex or sensitive environments. This approach enables DefendAir to serve as a practical kinetic interception
layer within multi-layered C-UAS architectures.
Operational Use Cases and Real-World Deployment
DefendAir is designed for
deployment across a range of real-world operational scenarios in which close-range protection against hostile drones is required and engagement
timelines are limited. Such scenarios include the protection of military personnel and units operating in forward or fixed positions,
security forces responsible for area protection, and the safeguarding of critical infrastructure, sensitive facilities, and high-value
assets.
In these environments, hostile
drones may approach at low altitude, high speed, and with minimal warning, reducing the effectiveness of long-range interception systems.
DefendAir is intended to provide a localized defensive capability that can be positioned close to the protected asset or personnel, enabling
rapid response to short-range threats.
The system is particularly
suited for environments where the use of traditional air defense or electronic warfare solutions may be impractical, restricted, or operationally
undesirable. These environments may include urban areas, civilian locations, transportation hubs, industrial facilities, and other sites
with elevated safety and collateral-risk considerations. In such settings, the use of explosive munitions, high-energy projectiles, or
wide-area electronic interference may be constrained due to regulatory, safety, or operational limitations.
DefendAir is designed to operate
as the final interception layer within a broader, multi-layered C-UAS architecture. In this role, the system provides a physical interception
capability when detection, tracking, or soft-kill measures such as electronic disruption fail to neutralize the threat. This layered deployment
concept reflects current C-UAS operational doctrine, which increasingly emphasizes redundancy, flexibility, and controlled engagement
across different threat profiles.
Advantages
Relative to Other C-UAS Solutions
Compared to alternative C-UAS
approaches, DefendAir offers several operational advantages that address limitations commonly associated with both soft-kill and traditional
hard-kill systems. Its non-explosive, net-based interception method is designed to physically neutralize hostile drones while minimizing
the risk of collateral damage and unintended secondary effects. This controlled interception approach is particularly relevant in populated
areas, sensitive facilities, and environments where safety considerations constrain the use of high-energy or explosive countermeasures.
DefendAir is intended to address
operational scenarios in which soft-kill solutions may be ineffective or unreliable. Electronic warfare and cyber-based C-UAS measures
may be limited against autonomous drones, pre-programmed flight paths, or systems designed to operate with reduced reliance on external
communications or navigation signals. In such cases, a physical interception capability provides an additional layer of assurance.
In addition, DefendAir is designed to offer a
cost-effective alternative to high-cost missile-based or projectile-based interception systems, particularly in close-range defense scenarios
involving small drones. This cost structure may support more sustainable deployment for point defense, perimeter protection, and repeated
engagements, without the cost asymmetry often associated with traditional air defense solutions.
Together, these characteristics
position DefendAir as a practical solution for close-range C-UAS applications that require precision, controlled engagement, and rapid
response within constrained operational environments.
43
Overview
of the DefendAir Product Portfolio
The DefendAir product portfolio
comprises multiple configurations designed to address a range of operational requirements, threat profiles, and deployment scenarios.
Each configuration is based on the same core net-based interception technology and is adapted to specific use cases and operational environments.
●Hand-Held Net Launcher
A portable, operator-controlled system
designed for personal protection and point defense against fast-approaching drones, including FPV threats. This configuration is intended
for use by military personnel, security forces, and protection units requiring a rapidly deployable, close-range defensive capability.
●Turret-Based System
A fixed or vehicle-mounted configuration
designed to support perimeter defense and protection of critical assets, facilities, and infrastructure. This configuration is intended
for deployment at fixed sites or on mobile platforms, providing localized C-UAS coverage in areas requiring continuous or semi-persistent
protection.
●Integrated Drone Interception Configurations
DefendAir systems are designed for integration
within layered C-UAS architectures. These configurations provide a close-range physical interception capability that complements detection,
tracking, and soft-kill measures, enabling interception of residual threats in complex operational environments.
DropAir – Precision Airdrop and Aerial Delivery Solution
Use Case
DropAir is our precision
aerial delivery solution designed to enable controlled, accurate deployment of payloads from UAS in operational environments where ground
access is limited, unsafe, or impractical. The system is intended to support delivery of mission-critical supplies, equipment, and payloads
to designated ground locations while reducing risk to personnel and assets.
DropAir is designed for use
in military, security, humanitarian, and emergency response scenarios, including resupply of forward or isolated units, delivery into
contested or constrained areas, and deployment in environments where conventional logistics methods may expose personnel to elevated risk.
By enabling stand-off delivery from aerial platforms, DropAir is intended to enhance operational flexibility and reduce reliance on ground-based
transport under hostile or hazardous conditions.
44
Origin and Development
DropAir
was developed in response to an operational request from the Israel Defense Forces for a controlled and reliable aerial delivery capability
using unmanned platforms. The request reflected a need for precision delivery of payloads in complex operational environments, where accuracy,
reliability, and controlled descent were critical requirements.
We
applied our existing expertise in autonomous safety systems, controlled deployment mechanisms, and aerospace-grade design to develop a
solution tailored to these operational needs. The development of DropAir leveraged our experience in real-time activation logic, deployment
timing, and mitigation of uncontrolled descent, adapting these capabilities from safety applications to precision delivery use cases.
This
origin shaped DropAir’s design priorities, emphasizing predictability, operational reliability, and suitability for deployment in
real-world defense and security scenarios.
Capabilities
DropAir is designed to provide
controlled aerial delivery of payloads with a focus on accuracy, stability, and operational safety. The system enables release and descent
of payloads in a controlled manner, reducing drift and impact energy relative to uncontrolled free-fall delivery.
The system is intended to
be compatible with a range of unmanned aerial platforms and configurable for different payload characteristics and mission requirements.
DropAir is designed to support delivery in varied environmental conditions and operational contexts, allowing operators to tailor deployment
parameters based on mission needs.
By combining controlled descent
with autonomous deployment logic, DropAir is intended to support precision delivery missions while reducing operational risk and improving
mission effectiveness in environments where traditional resupply or delivery methods may be constrained.
Commercial Milestones
The market for safety systems
for commercial drones is rapidly evolving and subject to regulatory frameworks around the world that are in various stages of development
and sophistication. We have played a key role, as a leader in parachute safety systems, in the development of both the technology and
regulations around safe UAS operations.
The global C-UAS market has
been evolving rapidly, driven by the increasing proliferation of commercial and consumer drones, the growing use of unmanned systems in
asymmetric conflicts, and heightened concerns around the protection of critical infrastructure, public events and military assets. In
the past two years, we invested in research and development of our C-UAS technology and solutions to address these evolving operational
and security requirements. We also recognized strong and increasing demand from defense end users for solutions that are modular, rapidly
deployable, interoperable with existing command-and-control systems, and capable of detecting, identifying and mitigating a broad range
of drone threats in complex and contested environments.
45
Below are some recent regulatory and commercial
milestones that we have been involved in:
Regulatory Milestones
In October 2023, we announced
that the Australian Civil Aviation Safety Agency authorized drones to operate over populated area and near people when using our safety
systems, the first such authorization of its kind in Australia. The approval was obtained by our Australian regional partner, OVRL, whose
tailored safety case and Specific Operations Risk Assessment, or SORA, application helped facilitate the landmark approval, which now
paves the way for all organizations throughout Australia to benefit from similar operational approvals
In January 2024, we announced
that we facilitated one of our customers in obtaining the first-ever light uncrewed aircraft system operator certificate, or LUC, in Denmark.
The LUC is an organizational approval certificate granted by the EASA, which is an agency of the European Union with responsibility for
civil aviation safety, that allows for cross-border operations throughout the European Union without additional approvals required, enabling
flight operations to be self-authorized by the LUC holder anywhere throughout EASA member states. Additionally, the LUC holder may operate
a variety of UAS platforms under one single approval, offering a quantum change in the efficiency of drone aerial services, while maintaining
safe operating conditions. Our SafeAir parachute system was utilized throughout the LUC application process to enable a broader range
of advanced flight permissions, including operations over people, considered to be a highly sought-after flight permission.
In November 2024 we announced
that we received a Design Verification Report, or DVR, approval from EASA, for the SafeAir M-300 Pro and SafeAir M-350 Pro parachute safety
kits. This approval added to our portfolio of previously granted approvals from the Federal Aviation Administration, or FAA, alongside
additional territories. The EASA DVR confirms that our SafeAir M-300/ M-350 Pro parachute systems comply with key safety requirements,
enabling drone operators to enhance their operational scope under the SORA process.
In January 2025, we announced
today that we received official approval from the Israeli Defense Export Controls Agency (DECA) under the Israel Ministry of Defense for
the marketing of the DefendAir C-UAS solution.
In April 2025, we received
a marketing approval from the Israeli Ministry of Defense’s DECA for the DropAir™ Precision Airdrop System, developed in collaboration
with Heven Drones, a leading U.S. drone manufacturer with roots in Israel that specializes in custom autonomous UAS platforms. This authorization
from DECA enabled us and Heven to actively market our joint DropAir-integrated solution to global clients across commercial, defense,
and humanitarian sectors.
In August 2025, we announced
that we received official marketing approval from the Israeli Ministry of Defense’s DECA for the DropAir™ Precision Airdrop
System, integrated with advanced unmanned aerial platforms developed by Steadicopter Ltd., a leading innovator in the rotary unmanned
aerial systems (RUAS) industry.
Commercial Milestones
In January 2025, we successfully
launched a pilot program utilizing our DropAir precision airdrop system in a high-risk operational zone. The program, conducted in collaboration
with a leading drone company, demonstrated the DropAir system’s ability to deliver critical blood transfusions rapidly and safely,
significantly reducing the time needed to save lives in emergency situations.
In February 2025, we announced
that a leading drone solutions provider, utilizing our safety technology, secured an FAA waiver to conduct BVLOS drone operations, which
illustrated the critical role that our safety systems in enabling complex drone missions that push the boundaries of traditional operational
limits.
In March 2025, we announced
the expansion of a strategic partnership with ABOT, one of France’s largest drone distributors of advanced drone solutions for various
industries, to expand the availability of its cutting-edge SafeAirTM parachute recovery systems in the French market. Under this collaboration,
ABOT became an official reseller of our SafeAir products in France, with the two companies jointly launching a new brand, ABOT-PZ SafeAir,
to align with local market preferences.
In July 2025, we completed
a live demonstration of our DefendAir Personal Net Gun System to a select group of Israeli security and defense professionals. During
the live field simulation, the DefendAir system demonstrated 100% interception success, effectively neutralizing every fast-incoming multirotor
drone threat in real-time scenarios.
46
In September 2025, we successfully
completed a field trial of its DefendAir Stationary Turret system with Israel’s homeland security authority. The trial demonstrated
the system’s effectiveness in safeguarding critical infrastructure and sensitive facilities by sites using our patented net interception
method mounted on a turrent.
In October 2025, we announced
the signing of a significant purchase order with Airobotics Ltd., a premier provider of robotic automation solutions, for the delivery
of our advanced safety systems. The purchase order is part of an ongoing collaboration between us and Airobotics, building on various
previous orders, including or C-UAS solutions
In November 2025, we received
a significant purchase order for our DefendAir anti-drone defense systems from a Dutch distributor, one of Europe’s largest integrators
that serves as a leading supplier of defense and homeland security (HLS) applications.
In December 2025, we successfully
demonstrated our DefendAir C-UAS system at a high-profile event organized by the International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT)
at the Israel Ministry of Defense’s (IMOD) demonstration facility in Israel. The demonstration showcased our DefendAir technology

In December 2025, we signed
a distribution agreement with a leading Western European distributor specializing in advanced defense systems and force training solutions,
which grants the distributor exclusive rights to distribute our DefendAir C-UAS across multiple Western European countries. The distributor
is a well-established player with extensive experience in distribution, integrating advanced defense systems, and providing specialized

In January 2026, we successfully
completed a live demonstration of the DefendAir C-UAS platform on European soil, which was held in partnership with a premier Western

In January 2026, we entered
into a reseller agreement with Lella Kentonis Investment Co. Limited, or Lella Kentonis, a specialist in homeland security equipment.
Lella Kentonis was appointed as our reseller in Cyprus, granting rights to distribute and integrate our product lines into the Cypriot

In January 2026, we entered
into an additional reseller agreement with a prominent Western European partner, marking another step in our strategic expansion
throughout Europe, particularly within major NATO-aligned defense markets.
In January 2026, we announced
the receipt of the first purchase order from a main Israeli defense entity for the DefendAir solution.
In February 2026, we announced
the receipt of an additional order from a second branch at an Israeli defense entity for the DefendAir solution. The order included:
●Specialized Launchers: High-precision
net-launchers designed for rapid deployment in urban and field environments, enabling soft-kill interception of hostile drones with minimal
collateral damage.
●Interception Pods: net-pods compatible
with handheld, stationary, and drone-mounted configurations, providing layered defense for troops, convoys, and critical infrastructure.
●Training Package: A comprehensive suite
of simulation-based and live-fire training modules to ensure operational readiness, including system integration, maintenance, and tactical

Our sales and marketing strategy
is focused on increasing brand awareness, supporting market education, and generating demand across our solutions in the defense and commercial
markets. Our approach emphasizes consistent engagement with customers, partners, and industry stakeholders, with the objective of positioning
us as a provider of specialized, mission-critical solutions within the C-UAS and unmanned aviation markets.
Marketing activities are executed
through a structured, year-round program that combines digital content, public communications, and direct market engagement. These activities
include the regular publication of educational and informational content, ongoing public relations efforts, and sustained presence across

In addition, we invest in
maintaining and updating its brand assets and marketing infrastructure, including corporate messaging, digital platforms, and sales enablement

of customer engagement across regions.

Competition and Competitive Landscape
The C-UAS market is highly
fragmented and characterized by a wide range of solution types, technology maturity levels, and go-to-market approaches. Based on internal
market analysis, competitors generally fall into three primary categories: (i) tactical point solutions, (ii) interceptor-based or net-capture
systems, and (iii) full-stack, integrated C-UAS platforms.
A number of competitors offer
tactical net-based or handheld interception tools designed primarily for short-range or point defense use. These solutions are typically
lower cost and simpler to deploy but are often limited in range, scalability, and integration into broader C-UAS architectures. Such products
are generally optimized for narrow threat profiles, including small or slow drones, and may lack the operational flexibility or system-level
integration required for larger defense or infrastructure protection programs.
Other competitors focus on
interceptor-drone–based systems, in which an autonomous drone is used to pursue and capture hostile drones, often using a net-based
mechanism. These systems may offer controlled capture and recovery capabilities but typically rely on airborne interception platforms,
which can introduce operational complexity, higher costs, and dependency on supporting detection, command-and-control, and airspace management
infrastructure. Many of these offerings are early-stage or limited in production scale and field history.
At the higher end of the market,
several competitors provide full-stack C-UAS solutions that combine proprietary sensors, command-and-control software, and kinetic or
non-kinetic interceptors. These systems are often marketed as comprehensive airspace defense platforms and may offer broad coverage and
integration. However, such solutions are typically associated with higher acquisition and lifecycle costs, longer deployment timelines,
and increased complexity, which may limit their suitability for certain customers or use cases, particularly those requiring rapid deployment
or localized protection.
Based on our internal competitive
assessment, we operate in an intermediate segment of the market, positioned between single-purpose tactical tools and large, fully integrated
C-UAS systems. Our DefendAir solutions are designed to provide a controlled, close-range kinetic interception capability that can function
as a stand-alone point defense solution or be integrated into multi-layered C-UAS architectures. This positioning is intended to address
operational requirements that are not fully met by low-end tactical tools or high-cost, system-level platforms.
Competition in this market
is influenced by factors including technological performance, operational suitability, cost, ease of integration, regulatory constraints,
export controls, and customer procurement preferences. We expect competition to remain intense as drone threats evolve and as both established
defense contractors and emerging technology providers continue to invest in C-UAS solutions.

Research and Development and Future Applications
We devote substantial resources
to research and development with the objective of developing new products and technologies and reducing unit costs of our products. Our
development strategy is to identify products for material, hardware and software that enhance and improve the performance of our solutions
for our customers. We measure the effectiveness of our research and development by metrics, including product unit cost, efficiency, reliability,
optical performance, customer adoption and customer surveys.
We are actively advancing
our research and development pipeline to address the evolving global threats posed by UASs, particularly the proliferation of FPV “suicide”
drones. Our future growth strategy is centered on the following key development pillars:
1.Personnel Protection Systems: We are developing a
compact, personal net-launching system designed for soldier protection. This modular solution is engineered to be wearable on tactical
vests or mounted as an add-on on personal firearms, providing a critical “last-meters” kinetic defense against low-altitude
FPV threats.
2.Perimeter Defense & Armored Vehicle: Leveraging
our proprietary net-pod technology, we are engineering specialized systems for the protection of high-value assets and Armored Fighting
Vehicles (AFVs), including tanks and APCs. We believe this represents a significant market opportunity, addressing a critical vulnerability
gap in modern maneuver warfare where traditional defenses struggle against small, agile loitering munitions.
3.Non-Explosive Tactical Defense System: We are developing
a comprehensive, short-range tactical defense system (effective up to several hundred meters). By utilizing a mechanical net-deployment
mechanism rather than traditional ballistics or explosives, this system offers a low-cost, low-collateral-damage solution ideal for sensitive
civilian environments, critical infrastructure, and military protection.
4.Interceptor Drone Integration: We are expanding our
strategic collaborations with international drone manufacturers and partners to integrate our net-pod launchers onto third-party interceptor
drones. This capability provides a highly effective, reusable interception method suitable for both military and Homeland Security (HLS)
scenarios.
5.Air Dropped Logistics System - DropAir: Building upon
our success with the Israel Ministry of Defense and the IDF Medical Corps—where our system was pioneered for the precision delivery
of fresh blood transfusions to the battlefield—we are evolving the DropAir platform. Our goal is to create a platform-agnostic,
“plug-and-play” logistical drop system. This will allow commercial and military operators to rapidly convert existing UAV fleets
into precision delivery assets for medical supplies and critical equipment.

We also engage with domestic
defense contractors and international aerospace partners in connection with system development, integration, and validation activities.

Through this structure, we

Government Regulation
The use of UAS is heavily
regulated and, as is often the case with developing technologies, the design, manufacture, and operation of UAS are subject to extensive
regulation by aviation, telecommunications, national security, and privacy authorities in the jurisdictions in which we operate. Regulatory
frameworks governing drones continue to evolve rapidly as governments seek to integrate unmanned aircraft into national airspace systems
while ensuring public safety, national security, and privacy protections.The regulation of the operation and flight of UAS around the
world is lagging behind the industry’s technological capabilities. Many countries and governments, such as the United States
and the European Union, have developed regulations that prohibit the use of UAS in urban or populated environments, except in specific
scenarios and/or with appropriate air and ground risk mitigation measures, including the use of parachutes.
Our operations are subject
to extensive and evolving laws and regulations in the jurisdictions in which we operate, particularly those relating to defense and security
technologies, UASs, C-UAS technologies, export controls, cybersecurity, and government procurement. These regulations may affect the development,
manufacture, marketing, sale, export and deployment of our products and technologies.
Defense and Security Regulations
Because certain
of our products and technologies may be used for defense, homeland security, or law enforcement purposes, our business is subject to regulations
governing the development, testing, production, marketing and sale of defense-related technologies. These regulations may include licensing,
registration, classification, and oversight by national defense or security authorities in the countries where we operate.
In many jurisdictions, companies
engaged in the development or supply of defense-related technologies are required to obtain approvals or licenses from relevant governmental
authorities before engaging in certain activities, including manufacturing, marketing or exporting controlled technologies. Compliance
with these regulations may impose administrative, operational and reporting obligations on our business.
United States
U.S. government agencies,
including the Defense Contract Audit Agency and the Defense Contract Management Agency, routinely audit government contractors. These
agencies review the performance of companies under contracts, cost structure and compliance with applicable laws, regulations and standards,
as well as the adequacy of and such companies’ compliance with its internal control systems and policies.
The drone industry is regulated
in the United States by the FAA to ensure that drone related services meet safety and performance standards. The FAA prescribes standards
and certification requirements for use of UAS for commercial and recreational purposes. The rule for operating UAS under 55 pounds in
the U.S. national airspace is the FAA’s Small UAS Rule (14 CFR Part 107). On April 21, 2021, the FAA’s Operation
of Unmanned Aircraft Systems Over People final rule (14 CFR Part 107 Subpart D) went into effect, allowing for routine drone operations
over people under certain circumstances. Under these rules, the FAA categorizes UAS operations over people depending on the level of risk
that the UAS presents to people on the ground. Parachute recovery systems mitigate ground risk in the event of an in-flight emergency
by significantly reducing the kinetic energy of a falling aircraft.
Since 2019, hundreds of FAA
§107.39 waivers have been granted for operations over people using SafeAir technology, including to organizations such as Hensel
Phelps, the Chicago Police Department, Verizon Media, The New York Times and State Farm Insurance. These waivers allow small UAS
which do not meet the four operational categories mentioned above to be flown over human beings.

Israel
We
may be subject, both directly and indirectly, to the adverse impact of existing and potential future government regulation of our products,
technology, operations and markets. In Israel, the drone sector is regulated principally by the Civil Aviation Authority of Israel under
the Israeli aviation regime, together with operational restrictions published through the national aeronautical information system. At
the policy level, Israel continues to develop its broader unmanned-aircraft regime against a backdrop of both commercial enablement and
security concerns. Public Israeli materials indicate ongoing regulatory attention to drone registration, pilot licensing and integration
of drones into the national airspace system, while state oversight bodies have also noted the importance of completing the regulatory
framework for effective enforcement and safer integration.
Export Controls and International
Trade Regulations
Many of our products, components
and technologies are subject to export control and trade compliance laws and regulations in the jurisdictions where they are developed
or manufactured. These regulations may restrict or require licenses for the export, re-export or transfer of certain hardware, software,
technical data or services to foreign countries, governments or persons.
In particular, we are subject
to Israeli defense-related export controls. The marketing and export of defense related equipment, services, ‘know-how’ are
subject to the Israeli Defense Export Control Agency within the Israeli Ministry of Defense, or DECA, regulation under the Defense Export
Control Law, 5766-2007, or the Export Control Law and, collectively, Israeli Trade Control Laws, which impact our operations, for example
by limiting our ability to sell, export, or otherwise transfer our products or technology, or to release controlled technology to non-Israeli
companies.
Under the Export Control Law,
an Israeli company may not conduct “defense marketing activity” without a defense marketing license from the Israeli Ministry
of Defense, and may be subject to a requirement to obtain a specific license from the Israeli Ministry of Defense for any export of defense
related products and/or knowhow. The definition of defense marketing activity is broad and includes any marketing of “defense equipment,”
“defense knowhow” or “defense services” outside of Israel, which includes “dual-use goods and technology,”
(material and equipment intended in principle for civilian use and that can also be used for defensive purposes, such as certain of our
products) that is specified in the list of Goods and Dual-Use Technology annexed to the Wassenaar Arrangement on Export Controls for Conventional
Arms and Dual-Use Goods and Technologies, if intended for defense use only, or is specified under Israeli legislation. “Dual-use
goods and technology” will be subject to control by the Israeli Ministry of Economy if intended for civilian use only.
In addition, under the Export Control Law,
the Israeli Ministry of Defense and DECA have various audit and supervision powers to ensure compliance with the Export Control Law, to
which violations are subject to criminal and administrative penalties. We are also required to submit periodic reports to DECA, and to
maintain and retain records as to the information and documents pertaining to defense export transactions conducted.
The
failure to satisfy the requirements under the Israeli Trade Control Laws, including the failure or inability to obtain necessary licenses
or qualify for license exceptions, could delay or prevent the development, production, export, import, and/or in-country transfer of
products and technology.
In
addition, exports of certain aerospace, defense and C-UAS technologies may be regulated under export control regimes such as:
●the International Traffic in Arms Regulations
(ITAR) and the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) in the United States;
●European Union dual-use export control regulations;
●Israeli defense export control regulations administered
by the Defense Export Controls Agency (DECA); and
●similar regulatory frameworks in other jurisdictions.

Grants for Research and Development
Under the Israeli Encouragement
of Research, Development and Industrial Initiative Technology Law, 5744-1984, as amended, and the regulations promulgated thereunder,
or the Research Law, research and development programs which meet certain specified criteria and are approved by the IIA’s research
committee are eligible for grants which are determined as a percentage of the project’s expenditure, as determined by the IIA’s
research committee, in exchange for the payment of royalties from the revenues generated from the sale of products and related services
developed, in whole or in part pursuant to, or as a result of, a research and development program funded by the IIA. The royalties
are generally determined at a range of 3.0% to 6.0% of the project’s revenues until the entire IIA grant is repaid, together with
an annual interest. Until December 31, 2023, the interest was calculated at a rate based on the 12 months LIBOR Rate applicable to
dollar deposits that was published on the first business day of each calendar year, however, pursuant to the latest IIA regulations,
as of January 1, 2024, IIA grants received after June 30, 2017, shall bear interest calculated at a rate based on an annual application
of the SOFR, or at an alternative rate published by the Bank of Israel, plus approximately 0.72%; and, for grants approved on or following
January 1, 2024, the annual interest rate shall be the higher of (i) the 12 months SOFR interest rate plus 1%, or (ii) a fixed annual
interest rate of 4%.
The terms of the Research
Law also require that the manufacture of products developed with government grants be performed in Israel. The transfer of manufacturing
activity outside Israel may be subject to the prior approval of the IIA (the approval of the IIA is not required for transfer of no more
than 10% of the manufacturing capacity in the aggregate outside of Israel, though a notice must still be provided to the IIA in such case).
Under the regulations of the Research Law, assuming we receive approval from the Chief Scientist to manufacture our IIA-funded products
outside Israel, we may be required to pay increased royalties. The increase in royalties depends upon the manufacturing volume that is
